headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors: caveman can feed MCP/file content into a shell-capable RAG course agent with write access and allowlisted egress.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a uses MCP and reads/writes project files, while agent_b can execute shell commands and read/write the filesystem. That creates a plausible bridge where attacker-controlled content from caveman can reach the course agent’s tool-use path. Because neither profile shows provenance tracking or isolation, uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF agent_a outputs instructions into shared files or MCP messages that agent_b parses as trusted text
IF both agents are run in the same workspace without content provenance checks
mitigations: Disable shared-file handoff between agents for the run
Add a manual review step before agent_b executes any instructions from agent_a
Separate workspaces per agent
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging on all inter-agent artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches session logs, memory files, project notes, and CLAUDE.md; agent_b touches academic papers, metadata, research questions, and configuration secrets. A shared workspace or copied artifacts could leak sensitive material between them. The profiles do not prove a shared filesystem by default, so medium is the highest supported level.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share a workspace or exchanged files
IF agent_b is pointed at directories containing agent_a session logs or memory files
mitigations: Keep separate directories for each agent
Remove secrets from any shared folder before running
Restrict agent_b to a read-only subset of inputs
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem sandboxing

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_b has filesystem write and shell execution; agent_a has multiple-instance support and file-oriented surfaces. Even though agent_a’s write capability is not explicit, the pair can still contend over shared files or generated artifacts if co-located. Because shared-state locking is not stated, the conflict risk is real but not proven high.
conditions: IF both agents write into the same project directory
IF agent_b modifies files that agent_a later reads without locking
mitigations: Run agents in separate directories
Serialize file writes manually
Use read-only mounts for shared inputs
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a is a content-writing agent and agent_b exposes /api/v1/ask and /api/v1/agentic-ask, so A’s output can plausibly become B’s input. The profiles do not show a verification gate before B acts on A’s text, but they also do not prove autonomous downstream actions. That supports medium rather than high.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a’s generated text as authoritative context
IF agent_b forwards A’s output into downstream API calls or notebooks without review
mitigations: Require human review of agent_a outputs before reuse
Add a checklist for factual claims before agent_b acts
Limit agent_b to summarization rather than action-taking
requires-engineering: add verification prompts or validators

E_compliance.rationale: agent_b explicitly handles configuration secrets and requests Docker Desktop plus Airflow credentials, while agent_a touches session logs and memory files. If either agent processes regulated or secret-bearing data in a shared environment, retention and residency controls can diverge. The profiles do not show a specific residency mismatch, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data or secrets are stored in the same workspace as both agents
IF retention or deletion policies differ between the two environments
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared notebooks and logs
Document retention rules for each agent run
Use separate accounts or environments
requires-engineering: align logging and deletion policies
